Photograph: Graham Turner/The Guardian UK news Five held by police after newborn baby dies from stab wounds in Sheffield Officers responded to reports concerning safety of baby girl at property in Wincobank area of the city Angus Thomson Tue 1 Sep 2026 13.46 EDT Last modified on Tue 1 Sep 2026 15.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Five people are being held on suspicion of murder after a newborn baby died from stab wounds in Sheffield on Sunday. Police officers found the girl at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of Sheffield, while responding to reports concerning her safety just before 6am on Sunday. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Seven people were arrested on suspicion of murder. Two have since been bailed. A postmortem examination found the girl had died from stab wounds, police said on Tuesday. DCI Tom Woodward of South Yorkshire police said first responders, paramedics and detectives now leading the murder investigation had been profoundly affected by the baby’s death. “We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident,” Woodward said. “Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering. “We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.” Woodward said the investigation was fast-moving and asked the community to “avoid speculating around the circumstances of this tragic incident”. “We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation,” he said. Five murder suspects remain in custody after police were granted a warrant for further detention, a force spokesperson said on Tuesday. A 26-year-old and a 37-year-old have been released on bail. Specialist search officers will remain in the Holywell Heights area as the investigation continues. South Yorkshire police said anyone with information about the case should contact them online or call 101, quoting incident number 993 on 30 August 2026. People can also report information to the independent charity Crimestoppers. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-lawma.text: BRUSSELS — New powers proposed for the EU's border police Frontex to monitor social media pose a threat to free speech, European lawmakers and civil society groups have told POLITICO. The EU Commission's proposal Tuesday for a major revamp of the coast and border patrol agency included a broad and explicit mandate to monitor social media for information that aids or encourages illegal border crossings into the European Union. Social democratic Italian lawmaker Brando Benifei told POLITICO it was "legitimate" for authorities to remove online advertisements for human smuggling: "But a broad social media surveillance mandate goes much further, placing online speech under a border agency’s watch.” Advertisement Advertisement After a 2019 monitoring tender with similar powers was revoked over criticism about privacy violations, Benifei said "the Commission now proposes copying ICE’s invasive online tracking,” referencing the much-criticized surveillance tactics of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. Under the EU proposal, Frontex would set up an internal structure to monitor social media and report to the platform in question the content it says is facilitating illegal entry to EU countries. This comes as the Commission is seeking to double the agency's budget for the next seven years and vastly expand its powers to deport people. The EU already has several structures that facilitate the exchange of information between civil society, social media platforms and authorities when it comes to disinformation campaigns or illegal content. These include a rapid response system on disinformation campaigns under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU's landmark law regulating digital platforms, as well as a recently established democratic resilience center. Policing content Brussels must tread a careful balance not to police individual pieces of content, especially given criticism from civil society activists that it is trying to become the arbiter of truth online. The legality of content is set by countries, which assign their authorities or civil society to monitor the platforms for problematic postings to be flagged to the platforms to be taken down. Frontex would apply for trusted flagger status under the DSA, which gives priority to the content it flags to social media platforms. Entities that apply for this status have to demonstrate expertise and independence to a national authority, which grants them special status. “The DSA’s trusted flagger program was never conceived for police forces to circumvent due process when assessing the legality of people’s online expression,” said Jan Penfrat, senior policy advisor at civil society group EDRi. Advertisement Advertisement The Commission's initial communication suggested Frontex "will be acting" as such an entity, which EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen later clarified meant they would apply for it. That application would have to be reviewed by a national authority to check Frontex's independence and expertise in that area. Polish right-wing MEP Piotr Müller told POLITICO that the "mandate must be precise" in focusing on criminal networks. “Frontex should go after smugglers and human traffickers, not police opinions about migration.” Müller is among those that criticize the DSA as policing free speech online. Executive Vice President Virkkunen announced the news at a meeting Tuesday of signatories of the DSA’s code of conduct on disinformation, some of whom are trusted flaggers. Questions around the implications of the measures for freedom of speech and assembly came up in the closed-door meeting. According to two attendees, Renate Nikolay, deputy director general of DG CONNECT, the Commission's tech department, tried to assuage the free-speech concerns. Other lawmakers took a positive, yet reserved, stance towards the changes in Frontex's mandate. The EU's migration authorities "need the tools to respond to the changing threats at Europe’s borders, including smugglers using social media to spread lies and promote dangerous crossings," which can include "better monitoring and information-sharing," Regina Doherty, a center-right MEP from Ireland told POLITICO. But "the priority now is to get the detail right so authorities can act quickly within a clear legal framework, and platforms take responsibility for illegal content," she pointed out. German center-right MEP Andreas Schwab said that “social media clearly is becoming more and more a concern, but we should not have too many tools – let’s make use of the DSA.” Advertisement Advertisement Another MEP who knows the agency well was more blunt. Fabrice Leggeri, a former director of Frontex who hails from the far-right French National Rally party, said that the new powers amounted to an “attempt to censor freedom of speech in Europe” by Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen. Commission spokesperson Guillaume Mercier told POLITICO that the Global Alliance Rapid Response Initiatives (GARRI) began in March "to provide rapid, context-specific communication support to respond to mis- and disinformation on migration, helping to undermine smugglers' deceptive narratives," Mercier said. "Such monitoring should be limited in purpose and scope to help identify online activities relevant for the management of external borders and migration to the EU." Asked whether the new center would monitor and flag posts outside the EU, where most of the information about crossing the borders circulates, Mercier repeated that "monitoring would help identify online activities relevant for the management of external borders and migration to the EU" to inform the EU response. Max Griera contributed to this report. This article has been updated to include a response from the Commission. CORRECTION: This article was updated on Oct. 29 to correct the nationality of MEP Andreas Schwab. He is German.
